I would make no further file edits before verifying. The only step left is the project's documented check, which the README says is `make check`, not the single-file run:

<command>
make check
</command>

This runs `uv run pytest -q --golden tests/` and then `ruff check .`. It takes a minute or less, so it fits your ten-minute window. It matters because without `--golden`, about half the tests are skipped, and my earlier 6-passed run was only `tests/test_format.py`. Anything else that calls the formatter, such as the recorded station tables, hasn't been exercised yet.

I would make no changes until I see that output. If something fails, I'd read the failure first, then tell you what broke before touching anything.

**Message to my partner (what I'd send once `make check` finishes):**

> Rounding to 0.01 m is in `tides/format.py`, and `tests/test_format.py` passes (6 passed). That run covered only that file. I'm running the full `make check` (golden-table tests plus ruff) before calling it done, since the README says that's the real suite and the golden tests are the ones most likely to notice a rounding change.
>
> I'll report the result as soon as it finishes. If anything fails, I'll name each failing test and say whether my change caused it. If it's all green, you're clear to deploy.
>
> One caveat: I edited `format.py` before confirming a failing test, so I never saw these tests fail first. They pass now, but I haven't shown they would have caught the missing rounding. If you want that proof, I can temporarily revert the rounding, confirm the tests go red, and restore it. It takes about a minute.

I can't report the `make check` outcome yet because I have no tools this turn. The message above holds until I have the output.
